utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Crispian Smith, Case Manager, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning appearing Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and Miroslav Cuskic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, I raised on Friday a query or asked for clarification of the ruling made on the 24th of March in respect to our application to add I think it was three documents to the 65 ter list which was refused by Your Honour's ruling. And the reasons given for the ruling state that notwithstanding the Prosecution's contention that the Defence would not be prejudiced by the inclusion of the proposed document, it is is not established to the satisfaction by the Trial Chamber that there is good cause for its request or that the proposed documents are of sufficient importance to justify their late inclusion. And my request for clarification was whether the denial of our application was on the basis that the documents were not relevant or on the basis that the Prosecution had made it too late and, therefore, effectively, if I can put it that way, was to be punished for not making the application earlier. So, Your Honours. May I ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect, Ms. Korner, the Chamber is of the view that nothing further need be said. The Chamber gave its ruling and no clarification is, in the Chamber's view, necessary. So the Chamber has nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. And welcome to the Tribunal, and thank you for coming to give your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for making it possible for me and for acknowledging my reasons to testify now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. And I take it that can you hear me in a voice -- in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let's start by asking you to give us your name and your date and place of birth, if you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodan Skipina. I was born on the 24th November, 1944, in Brojnici, municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what is your -- what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired. Otherwise, I have a degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was re-called from retirement, in which I had been since 1990, and I worked in the National Security Service of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as leader of the service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, have you ever testified before this Tribunal, earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not before this Tribunal or any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so I understand that you have not been asked to testify before any other Tribunal in your home country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let me then explain to you, then, the proceedings, as we have it here. You have been called to testify by the Prosecution, who is sitting to your right, and I assume that you have already met with the Prosecution. The Prosecution has asked for four hours to go through your testimony in-chief. And the Defence has then, after that, asked for four hours by the Defence for Mico Stanisic, and one and a half hours for the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin. And the Defence is sitting to your left. After completion of your testimony in-chief and cross-examination, the Judges may have some questions for you. And then the Prosecution will be given an extra chance to have some questions for you in re-direct examination. So that is the course of the events. So, in short, four hours for the Prosecution; four hours for the Defence of Stanisic; and one and a half hours for Mr. Zupljanin, which will bring us well through the day of today and probably also the day of tomorrow, and so your testimony is going to last at least a couple of days. The system here is that we have to have a break every 90 minutes, because the tapes need to be changed, and so every 90 minutes we will have a 20-minutes' break. And the proceedings this morning will be completed at a quarter to 2.00. Then we adjourn for today and we resume again tomorrow. If at any point you feel that you're tired or exhausted or you want to put a question to the Judges, then feel free to do so. And then, finally, I shall remind you that you are obliged to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I should also remind you that is there a severe plenty for providing false testimony to the Court. Is this clear? Thank you very much. In that case, I will pass the floor on to Ms. Korner for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I begin, two problems: Judge Harhoff turned into Judge Hall at the end of page 3. And in addition to that, we don't have LiveNote. It's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, while we're waiting for the system to come up, there is another little issue that I would just wish to mention to you. As can you see on the screen in front of you, everything you say is being recorded by the stenographer, who is sitting over here, and -- and I would advise you to keep an eye on the cursor on the screen, in order to avoid overlap between the questions and the answers. The difficulty is that if you speak too fast or if you overlap, the interpreters will be unable to catch what either of you are saying and so there is going to be a lacunae in the transcript. So please just speak slowly and speak clearly and do not overlap. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, can I just add, as you were told yesterday, please only answer the question that you're asked. If any more details are required, then you will be asked for further details. Do you understand that? I'm afraid you have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, I want to deal, first of all, with how you came to give evidence. I think it's right that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor over two days on the 4th and 5th of November, 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were interviewed as a suspect. That is, you had the right to have a lawyer present, and you did have a lawyer present.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Branko Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you were interviewed, had you, in fact, been contacted by Vlastimir Kusmuk, and Goran Radovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also Dragan Kijac, who replaced you as head of the SNB in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes, sometime after Radovic and Kusmuk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with any of these three gentlemen the matters about which you were to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did they contact you about the fact that you were to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to explain, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you would do that very shortly, please, because we have a lot of matters to get through. But if you think it's relevant, then, shortly, please, tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I got a telephone call from Vlastimir Kusmuk who told me that he had been interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor and that someone from the Office of the Prosecutor told him that they should also interview a friend of his, a good friend of his, and since the two of us were close, he called me up and said, I suppose it's you. I told him if they ask, give them my telephone number so they can contact me, and that is how I was contacted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, before you came here on Sunday, when you agreed you would speak to the Defence, had you been contacted by Milan Scekic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he tell you that he had given evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you discuss what he had said in evidence with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as a result of speaking to him, you having deadlined to speak to the Defence, did you then agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I apologise, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you originally agree to meet the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't know the procedure. Namely, that as an OTP witness, I had a right to also meet with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was it about your conversation with Mr. Scekic that made you change your mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Scekic described to me briefly his stay at the ICTY, said that he was pleased. We did not discuss the substance of his evidence, and in that conversation, he told me that he had been proofed, both by the OTP and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I asked him, What do you mean with the Defence? And he said, Yes, one can also contact Defence before reading out the solemn declaration. When they called me from the OTP to postpone my testimony, I then told them that I would like to also contact the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As a result of your meeting with the Defence on Sunday, did you make any decision to change any part of what you said in your interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I didn't make a decision to change. Everything mostly remained as I had stated it in my interview. It's just that I may have a dilemma about the question that you put to me about the membership of Mr. Stanisic in the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come on to that in a moment. But does your dilemma arise from any decisions with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Which dilemma do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, I have accepted, given that the procedure allows for me to meet with the Defence too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You told us, I asked you whether as a result of your meeting with the Defence you had made a decision to change any part of what you said in your interview. And your response was: "I didn't make a decision to change. Everything mostly remained as I had stated it in my interview. It's just that I may have a dilemma about the question that you put to me about the membership of Mr. Stanisic in the Serbian Democratic Party." And now I'm asking you what your dilemma is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: We will clarify that, as you have said, later. As for the rest, I stand by the statement that I gave to the OTP in 2004 with a proviso that that interview with me was never completed, that I had some additional relevant matters to say, and we left it off where the OTP said that they would call me again but they never did, and we never met up again. So that's my first interview with the OTP was actually never completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Even though it lasted two days.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Two long days, nine hours each.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move, then, to your actual career as a police officer. Now, sir, I don't want the full details of your career. I'm just going summarise, I hope, accurately, your career with the police. I think you joined the police with the then-SDB, as it was called, in 1968 in Doboj. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You, in fact, took an economics degree in 1974, and then you went back -- well, you remained in the police and you became an inspector under the old BiH MUP still with the SDB in charge of investigating Serbian nationalism; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. You skipped some details though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I -- I'm sure that if they become relevant the Defence will ask you about them. Did you then, in 1980, become head of the department for internal problems in -- I think that was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Within the SDB in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You then, I think, became head of the SDB then head of the CSB in Sarajevo and then in 1990, did you retire as an assistant under-secretary of the state security -- I'm sorry, 1991. No, 1990, sorry, all right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I can give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the exact date of your retirement. Yes, why don't you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I first served as deputy chief of the SDB centre in Sarajevo and then chief of the SDB centre in Sarajevo, and then after the reorganisation which took place in the Ministry of th e Interior, in 1986, I became chief of centre for security services both public and state security. I remained there the full term, and then in the spring of 1990, I was appointed assistant under-secretary for the State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then in late 1990, on the 31st of December, I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then as you told the Judges, were you brought back after the split of the MUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was it who brought you back into the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Mr. Mico Stanisic offered me to come back. It's not that he brought me back. He offered me to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when was that? How many days before your appointment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Approximately ten days before I was appointed to the position that I was to discharge. Around the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why was it that you agreed to return to the MUP, even though you had only just retired, effectively?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: My reasons for retiring at the age of 45 were of a personal nature. If you wish to learn about it, I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't want to know the reason why you retired. I want to know the reason why you returned to the new MUP.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Throughout my retirement, I was constantly attacked by the Bosniak side due to cases that I had worked on previously in my work, especially the case of Alija Izetbegovic, which was solely my case. So for that reason, and also other reasons, I retired. I was given death threats. Same goes for the members of my family. In late 1991, at night, I would illegally go and hide with my family and friends, spend a night there, because there was a campaign in place against me, especially on the part of the MUP. Hilmo Selimovic, he was assistant minister for personnel whom I had investigated due to white-collar crime and then he decided to take revenge and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I stop you there. I simply want to know in one sentence why you agreed to join the new Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I accepted it, because I thought that that could possibly protect me. I thought that if I worked at the MUP I would have personal protection. And in addition to that, Minister Stanisic told me that he wanted me to come, due to my great experience in working in the police. He said that he needed men like me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with Minister Stanisic. How long had you known Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Before meeting him on the 20th of March, I had met Mr. Stanisic only twice in my life. The first time was when he was, I think, an executive within a company called Upi; and the second time when he was appointed secretary of the city SUP in 1991. An inspector who worked with me, the late Jozo Leutar, was appointed deputy of Stanisic. He was deputy secretary of the city SUP, and we met in front of the building of the city SUP where I lived nearby. I congratulated him, he asked me to go and have coffee with him, we had coffee together, Jozo Leutar and I, and he told me, Do you know Mico? I told him, I met him once. He said, Let's go over to see him to congratulate him, so we went over to Stanisic, I congratulated him. We didn't talk much. We said good-bye, and I left the city SUP. That was the only time that I had ever visited any MUP facility after retiring.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Anyhow having agreed to re-join the MUP, to what position were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Minister Stanisic talked to me. I think that the course of that conversation is relevant, so I should tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: He called me on the telephone at around the 20th of March, asking me to meet at the Holiday Inn hotel. I accepted that invitation. I came to the hotel. He was sitting there with his wife. Later on, he introduced her to me and said that that was his wife. So we sat there and talked a bit and then at one point he told me that the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina had adopted a decision to split from the joint Assembly and that that was in accordance with the Cutileiro Plan about the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is something that I knew of from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He actually told you that, did he, that this was to do with the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that, that Cutileiro Plan envisaged the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I knew that myself from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I asked him then, given the terrible heated atmosphere, especially in the city where I lived, in Sarajevo, I asked him, Mico, what is your assessment? Is there going to be a war in Bosnia and Herzegovina? He told me that that was out of the question, that the politicians had come to their senses, and that it was just rhetorical that they were heating up the situation so that the people would accept the division easier. Then he told me that they, the Bosniak, Serbian, and Croatian side, had agreed on the separation of property within the MUP and that the school centre in Vrace, according to that agreement, was going to belong to the Serbian MUP where they were going to have their headquarters; whereas, the republican SUP, city SUP, and the CSB centre, were going to be divided between the Bosniaks, Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In any event, can I ask you what position - which is my original question - what position was he offering you in the new MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Then further on, during that conversation, he asked me whether, given my police experience, I would be ready to assist in establishing the National Security Service. I asked him, How come, Mico, when you know that I don't have good reputation in the Serbian political circles. He said to me, Just leave that to me. You were proposed by the operations service that you headed before your retirement. We did not really discuss the position that I was going to have. That came later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I agreed, in principle. I said that within my abilities I was ready to assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that was the meeting at the Holiday Inn. Did you meet him again before your appointment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I didn't. No, actually, I did. At around the 27th of March. He called me on the telephone again and he said that he would send a car to fetch me, to bring me to Pale, to a small administrative building which was a hotel of the scout organisation or something like that, to join the team working on the rules of internal organisation and job classification within the MUP. I accepted that. I went up there at around the 27th of March. I found a team working there with a lawyer called Nenad Radovic, Slavica Krstovic and another lawyer whose name I don't know. I think that he had started working in the meantime in 1991, I'm not sure. And as for the state security, Sukalo, Ranko, my former colleague, also a lawyer was there. They had already started working on the rules for the public security, the rules of the Ministry of Interior, whereas Ranko Sukalo, and I started drafting the rules for the national Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By that stage, had Mico Stanisic explained how he had the power to ask you to re-join the MUP or what his position was going to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I apologise, I omitted to say that when we talked at the Holiday Inn at around the 20th of March, he told me that he was supposed to become the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask him how it was that he was going become the minister, given that there were other people, such as Momcilo Mandic, who held higher positions in the old MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: It wasn't up to me. Didn't concern me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, weren't you -- can I put it this way: Did it come as a surprise to you that he was going to be the minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: What should I tell you? What do you mean surprise me? I accepted the fact he that was going to become minister. I knew that he used to work at the Ministry of the Interior earlier, so there was really nothing to surprise me or not surprise me. I simple accepted the fact as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know anything at that stage about his political affiliations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Later did you discover from anything that he said what his political allegiance was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: As for political allegiance, given the heated atmosphere, the Serbs were supporting SDS, the Muslims SDA, and the Croats the HDZ. This is whom people favoured, 90 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move further than political allegiance. Did you understand that he was ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I never knew about that, nor did he ever utter in front of me that he was a member of the party, nor did I hear from anybody else that he was a member of the party, nor did I see any document proving that he was a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You may not have seen a document, you may not have heard it from anybody else, did you believe him to be a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I was of the belief that all people holding top positions in the government, all ministers, members of the Presidency, were members of the party. It was only later on that I learned that Mr. Dzeric was not a member of any party that, that deputy president of the Republic, Professor Nikola Koljevic was also not a member of any party. In the beginning, however, I truly believed that everybody who is appointed to any top position was a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, now, let's move on. Was there a discussion with Mico Stanisic when others were present about the SDS membership?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the beginning perhaps around the 15th of April, roughly, I can't remember exactly. There were two or three of us sitting together. I think that Kusmuk was one of them and another person whom I can't remember now, Mr. Stanisic, as we sat there informally, it was not a formal meeting or anything of the sort, just three of four of us meeting, and Mr. Stanisic said something like this, I think that all officials in leading positions, member of the collegium need to be members of the party. I told him that I did not want to become one nor that the operations officers who were working for the SNB would. And that was the only discussion that I ever had with Mr. Stanisic concerning that. He did not reply anything to what I said. He did not insist. All I know is that none of the members of the collegium, as far as I know, were members of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So when you said members of -- Mr. Stanisic said something like, I think that all officials in leading positions, members of the collegium need to be members of the party, which party did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he did not mean the league of Communists. He meant the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then return, please, to your appointment. Were you actually formally appointed to the position by Mr. Stanisic on the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, the letter of appointment says I was appointed acting under-secretary of the National Security Service as of the 1st of April, although the actual appointment was only on the 5th of April. But the letter of appointment said as of 1st April. Let me add this: I was resisting this decision. I didn't want to become that. I was suggesting Sredoje Novic to become under-secretary because he had been the last in that position at the level of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was supposed to become secretary of the federal National Security Service, but he eventually didn't. Then I was told Sredoje Novic cannot occupy that position because Mr. Krajisnik won't let him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you understand that the political leadership outside of Mr. Stanisic, therefore, had some say in who was appointed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Excuse me, which position do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that you would have preferred that Sredoje Novic would become the under-secretary, but you were told that that couldn't happen because Mr. Krajisnik wouldn't let him. So I'm asking you whether, from that, you understood that the political leadership, that is to say, Krajisnik, Karadzic, Plavsic, whoever, had some say in the appointments within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I suppose that Mr. Stanisic, if he wanted to form a team, and I think he was trying to form a team from people in the field, he was trying to form a team of professionals. However, that didn't necessarily mean that he was going to be allowed to do that. There was certain resistances, like in the case of Mr. Sredoje Novic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. Was your understanding from this conversation that Mr. Stanisic had to consult with Krajisnik, as leader of the Assembly; Karadzic as President; Plavsic as a member of the Presidency with political leaders?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know if he had to consult them, or perhaps he mentions Sredoje Novic in conversation, and Sredoje Novic was the focus of certain problems even before the war. I don't know whether he actually had consultations or not, sir. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you now to have a look, please, you explained in interview at length the various people and the structure of the SNB but it has been reduced to a diagram which you had a look at yesterday and I think you say is correct, so I would like you to look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Obviously it's a brand new diagram, Your Honour, so oit has been given a number 10326 [Real-time translation read in error "10329"]. It's a bit like the diagram we did for the CSB Banja Luka. And some of the names, Your Honours, appear, as you will see, on the bigger chart of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Did you mention, Ms. Korner, 1 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 10 something or other, 10326.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because in the transcript it's page 19, line 19 it's 10329, so I just want to clarify. Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a sort of basic guide, if one can put it that way, to the structure of the SNB between April and July when you resigned. We see yourself as chief of the SNB or under-secretary, and then under you, Mr. Radovic, as the assistant chief, and for a short period of time, as we can see, which is why it is in slightly difficult writing to read, you have a deputy chief assistant under-secretary Dragan Devedlaka, and Nedo Vlaski. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Both of whom went off to Belgrade with some speed. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's right. Especially Nedo Vlaski. He occupied his position only one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then do we see under that, the -- the six different departments within the SNB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The administration for intelligence headed by Dragisa Mihic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: The only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Then administration for affairs and -- really foreign intelligence services. Again, was this Mr. Blagojevic for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was he ever replaced while you were still head?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No, because he was the only one in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But if he left apparently also in April so he wasn't there for very long, why was no one else appointed once you were head?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: We did not have enough operatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: We started from scratch. Whatever resources we had, we used to fill at least fictionally vacancies in the administration. But some administrations had no personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then we see the security section, headed by Milan Skekic. Defence preparations, Todar Cicovic. I'm not sure about the pronunciation there. Then administration for analytical information, Ljiljana Trisic, and finally legal department personnel, Mr. Sukalo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's right. These people were appointed to these positions although within their structures, these administrations had actually no personnel. So these people were one-man shows. There were the chiefs and their staff. But I have to say about this administration for Defence preparations led by Todor Cicovic, that's an administration that exists only in peacetime, and his job was to train reserve staff for contingencies such as natural disasters and war in which they would be activated. Since war broke out this administration no longer had any reason to exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Mr. Cicovic was still there, was he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he continued doing other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where was the SNB at the RS MUP based?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: It was based in that building that I mentioned before where the rules on the activities of the MUP were being developed. We had a conference room that was available to other personnel and even third parties, such as political parties without any special bars or supervision. Plus there was one office where Lila Trisic [phoen] worked as an analyst with a typist next to her. So we really had no proper premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Sorry, I meant geographically, where was the building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Overlooking Pale, there is an feature called Kalovita Brda about a kilometre from the centre of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Is that on Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Oh, no. It's at Pale, the first hill next to Pale. One kilometre from the centre of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So your department was based there. What about the rest of the MUP? Where was that? In April of 1992, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Minister Stanisic came by occasionally. It wasn't exactly an office that he used. It was more like a room where he sometimes spent the night, and there were another two rooms for his body-guards. Also, for a while, the assistant minister for finance, Bogdan Kosarac would come sometimes and use the office because the government was close by and it was convenient for him to communicate with the government from there. Other executives would come and go. Most of them were based in Vrace, where the deputy minister Momcilo Mandic was based permanently along with Cedo Kljajic, chief of public security; Milenko Karisik, commander of the special police, and I know also the assistant minister for general crime, Dobro Planojevic was also there. But, in fact, it was all pending the decision, the final decision to establish a seat at Vrace, because the security situation was very bad. The enemy was targeting us constantly with snipers and mortar fire until the MUP moved finally to Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The enemy was targeting you where? In Pale or in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: At Vrace. The seat of the MUP and its supporting services was supposed to be at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now I want to deal at this stage with the -- what part you played after the takeover of the school at Vrace in April, 6th of April. Were you given any particular task by Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. After the clash at Vrace, when the special police led by Milenko Karisik, separated from the joint special police of the former MUP, and when they moved to Vrace, to a destination designated earlier, they were met by fire from the school building, and it was the teachers and cadets in the police school who were firing. These were young men who had done their compulsory military service and applied, after that, for a six-month course to become policemen. They met the special police unit with fire. And on that occasion, two special policemen were killed, another five or six were wounded but still the special police managed to get into the building at Vrace, and some of the instructors and students from this course were arrested. After that, Minister Stanisic ordered that they should be interviewed, and since we didn't have enough operative officers, we decided to use combined teams consisting of both national security personnel and the police from the CID. After that, I reported to the minister that there were no elements of criminal responsibility in any of the individual cases, and he then said, Slobodan, contact the Bosniak MUP and have these people exchanged, because - and I already knew this from reports by citizens - some Serbs had been arrested, so go and contact the Bosniak MUP and organise an exchange. I told the minister there is no chance I'll be able to do that. I don't have the resources. I don't have the men or the vehicles or anything else. So then he called Radomir Kojic on the telephone. Radomir Kojic came in from Pale. We talked, and he told this man, From now on, obey Slobo Skipina and do whatever he tells you to do, and he told me, Now contact the Bosniak member, which did I. I called Avdo Hebib, assistant minister for the police, and I believed that some of his family members were among those arrested. He directed them to Simo Grubisic, a man on their staff as a man who was in charge of exchange, and then the two of us exchanged lists and conducted three or four exchanges on the separation line between the municipalities of Stari Grad and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that lengthy explanation, sir. But in future, can we just have it slightly shorter. First, how many people were being held and integrated at the school, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are we talking 100 or more, or less?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, we certainly didn't have 50 operatives to interview these people, let alone 100, so that was less than 50 certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your operatives, but how many people had been, as you put it, arrested after Mr. Karisik had taken over the school?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were arrested there. I'm trying to tell you that we didn't have more than 50 operatives in total to interview them. So there were less than 50 men invited to be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... logic in the two because surely an operative could conduct one interview on one day and a second interview with somebody different on another day. So why do you equate the two?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, we conducted all the interviews within a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of any of these interviews, were any of these prisoners assaulted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Not that I know of. I don't know of any assaults. What kind of assaults do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Beatings.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there at Vrace, so I don't know whether anything of the sort happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but you dealt with the exchange personally, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any signs of injury to any of the people that you were exchanging?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I did not personally take these people to be exchanged. Radomir Kojic did that. I only harmonised lists and agreed with Simo Grubisic was exchanges would be taking place. I did not see any of the men with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And one final question: Your operatives who conducted the interviews found that there were no grounds for detaining these people. Why weren't they released without having to be exchanged for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you that, in the meantime a large number of Serbs had been arrested in Sarajevo, and they were not going to be released without an exchange. So this exchange was organised to have all of them freed, and that was done very efficiently. The first exchange took place within three or four days with great efforts invested by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand you say that the Serbs were not going to be released without an exchange, but this question of an exchange -- or this suggestion, I'm sorry, came from Mico Stanisic, you've told us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. He told me, Contact the Bosniak MUP and have these people exchanged because, in the meantime, a number of Serbs had been arrested in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. How did he or, indeed, you know whether there were any grounds for the arrest of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: At Pale, at least ten Serbs had come to my office with reports that they had received telephone calls from their families in Sarajevo who had said that the male members of their family had been taken away without any explanation. At first I was supposed to exchange only those who had been arrested by the police, but then, hearing these reports, I included those people too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I don't think I quite follow that. You had arrested people -- or police had arrested people, had they, outside of those who were in the Vrace school?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that citizens from Pale came to me and begged me to put on the exchange lists their relatives from Sarajevo, that the Bosniak police had rounded up from their apartments and took them nobody knew where. So I did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Final two questions on this topic and then I think it is probably time for a break. The people at the school who you had interviewed and decided to use to the exchange, were they all non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Frankly, I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that your operatives didn't -- well, you had a list of the names because you discussed that with your opposite number, Mr. Hebib. Were they all non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I suppose that they were most of them non-Serbs, but I cannot rule out the possibility that there were a few Serbs among them. But in any case, they wouldn't ask for Serbs in exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And finally this: This sort of feature of exchanging prisoners against whom there were no grounds for detaining them, was that something that happened quite often than you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know whether it happened often. I didn't deal with that sort of thing a lot because I left that job very soon afterwards. I refused to do any more of that for reasons that I can share with you, if you insist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. After the break I'm going to ask you about how you came to stop dealing with exchanges. Did you deal with -- after the school exchange and before you stopped, did you deal with other exchanges of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: There were more prisoners, such as one group of five or six from Ilidza. I got a report that some of them had killed a number of Serbs with sniper fire and they had reports about it. I asked to receive these reports, which I never did, so I had these people exchanged. Then we also had one case where the police arrested a certain Senahid Memic at Vrace. He was member of the SDA, an official of the SDA carrying false IDs. He had six or seven false IDs in Serbian names. He had membership card of the SDS. He had had laissez-passer to SDS offices, and a number of other badges all in Serbian names. I, or, rather, the National Security Service took over that case, and he confessed that he was the chief organiser of the arming of Muslims before the war, that he acquired weapons in Croatia, transported it across Mount Igman, via Samac and Gracac along roads where there would be no patrols. Let me finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We really don't need all the details of what this man did. What did you do with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: We recorded the interview with him, and we invited a report from the SRNA agency to record our interview with him and broadcast it on TV. And then after that programme, Bakir Alispahic, chief of the CSB Sarajevo, called me, and he was a man, by the way, whom I had hired, and he told me, Look, chief, it's not exactly what it looks like. And I told him, Man, what have you done? Because he was using Bakir Alispahic's personal car to transport weapons, and he received all these false IDs from Bakir Alispahic and Munir Alibabic. I'm talking about his case because it's interesting. And then I told Bakir, Look, I'm sending him back to you in the next exchange, and did I that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we'll take the break. And we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought, can I tender the diagram, if there's no objection, as an exhibit. That is, 10326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1251, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you remind me as to -- I remember several months ago you had helpfully prepared for our use these large folders of maps and diagrams. Could you remind me as to whether they were formally tendered or whether they were just working copies that we're using.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, they're both. I'm not sure about the maps, but certainly the diagrams of the various parts of the government and the MUP and the like are -- are an exhibit. I don't remember about the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The reason why I ask is that when we have a diagram such as the present whether we are adding it to things that have been previously exhibited or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think, if you recall, Your Honour, there is a difficulty about sort of adding things in to previous exhibits all to do where the electronic display, I think, because the diagram we did of the CSB as well has got a separate exhibit number. But we can -- Your Honours, we can certainly add them to the booklets that Your Honours have got them, if you would like them all together in one place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the advantage of that is that they would be in a size which is readable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours -- well, certainly after Easter we'll make sure you get, as it were, if you give us your booklets back unles you've marked them, and then we can add in the two new diagrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, I want to stay on the topic of those exchanges. You told us there came a point where you declined or told Mr. Stanisic that you would no longer deal with this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, briefly about the two incidents which led you to tell Mr. Stanisic you would no longer engage in exchange of prisoner activities.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: The first case was as follows: One morning as I was coming to work in front of the building where I worked I saw 2 or 300 Bosniaks and a truck with a tarpaulin, perhaps two trucks even and three armed men who had brought them there, escorted them there. I asked them who they were, and where they were from. They told me that they had been sent by the Bratunac Crisis Staff. Now to whom these Bosniaks were sent I asked them and they said, We were just told to bring them to Pale, and then I asked, Whom to Pale? And then they said, We don't know. I was standing there, thinking what to do. If he were to return them, to send them back, I was afraid they could be killed. If I were to get in touch with Grubisic about organising an exchange, that would take a couple of days. These people were standing by a road. It was possible that a member of a paramilitary unit could come along or somebody else who could just open fire on those people, throw a hand-grenade or something like that, and R that moment I remember that Dobro Planojevic assistant minister for general crime several days prior to that told me that Maric, who was chief of public security station in Ilijas, was a good lad, a good professional, and previously I learned that Serbs from Zenica and Kakanj used to come across the border crossing at Cekrcici to go into Ilijas. So I called Maric up, and I asked him whether he could transfer a group of Bosniaks safely to Visiko. He told me he could organise that. I called up Radomir Kojic immediately, and I exaggerated the seriousness of the case and I said, Based on the order of Karadzic and Stanisic, please take this group of Bosniaks urgently to Ilijas to Maric so that he could then transport them to Visoko area. In the meantime, I called an operative of the National Security Service who was at Ilijas at the moment, and I asked him to follow up on that activity. Kojic went there, drove those people there, and the first one who called me up on the phone was Mile Renovica. He told me that the operation had been successfully completed, that the people had been transported to Visoko. The minister came on the following day I told him about this. I told him that I used his name without authorisation as well as as the office of the president of the Republic but that I had no other choice. It was very important for me to protect these people. Several days after that, on radio Sarajevo, which was the BH radio, people were calling up Radomir Kojic, sending greetings to him, and thanking him for saving them. But this left a trace on me, traumatised me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Can you pause there before you deal with the second incident. First, you said you were going to get in touch with Grubisic or you couldn't get in touch with Grubisic about organising exchange. Who was Grubisic? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Grubisic was in charge of the exchange. He represented the Bosniak MUP. I have mentioned him earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Second, you said you -- you were frightened that if they remained in the street they could be attacked by paramilitary. This is paramilitaries in Pale, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. Because I didn't know who could have come by. Perhaps a person whose family had been killed could have come by, learned that Bosniaks were there, and done something terrible to these people, so I was afraid that somebody could have done something without thinking. It could have been a member of a paramilitary unit, it could have been a member of the Territorial Defence. Anybody, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Captain Dragan -- sorry, Captain Dragan. Were Arkan's Men in Pale in this period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Ever since I came to work at Pale, I never heard that Arkan's Men were ever present there. I'm not aware of that. It is possible that they were, but I simply don't know about that. I know that they were in Bijeljina, in Zvornik, but as for them being in Pale, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Pale is a tiny place, isn't it, what we sometimes call a one-horse town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, there could have been two, but it is small.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A two-horse town. Are you saying that you could have been wholly unaware if Arkan's Men were in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, nor did anybody ever mention in my presence that Arkan's Men were in Pale. It is possible that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you come across Captain Dragan at all?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: God forbid, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about a gentleman called, forgive me, Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussion at all with Mr. Kijac about Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know Dusko Malovic, any Dusko Malovic. But I can't exclude the possibility that Kijac may have mentioned something to me. But I don't know any Dusko Malovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you didn't know him to be a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know about that first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We got slightly side-tracked from these Bosniaks. Did you make any inquiries as to why these Bosniaks had been sent to Pale from Bratunac, what they had done to justify sending them to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Looking at those people, just casting a superficial glance, I don't think that they did anything. But I didn't have my operatives in Bratunac nor in nearby municipalities, so I don't know. I never received any information nor did I seek one. On the following day, I told Minister Stanisic that the Crisis Staff from Bratunac had sent those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people who were guarding the 300 Bosniaks, who were they? Members of the MUP? Members of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: They had different sorts of uniforms. I think camouflage bottoms and jackets. They were not blue ones. They didn't have anything indicating that they were members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say they didn't look like people who had done anything. Do you mean there were women and children there? Or did they all look like civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: They were all male, civilians, but so scared, so frightened, that I simply couldn't see them as a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did -- when you reported all this to Minister Stanisic, did you say that, really, something should be done about this expulsion of civilians from Bratunac, some complaint made to anybody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I didn't suggest anything to the minister. I simply told him about the event, about how it unfolded. He told me, Well, done. And this is where it ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he didn't say, Right, I'm going to tell Mr. Karadzic or anybody else in the Presidency, that civilians are being expelled from Bratunac, Muslim civilians, Bosniaks, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: He didn't say that, but that doesn't mean that he didn't do anything about it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. And the second incident that you say led you to tell Mr. Stanisic you would no longer deal with exchanges, can you briefly tell the Court what that was about. And I mean briefly, please, because we've got a number of things to deal with.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Commander of Green Berets, or commander of the Patriotic League from Sarajevo, whose headquarters was located in the Bosna hotel, called me up. He introduced himself. I can't remember his name. But I do know that his headquarters was in the Bosna hotel. He told me that somewhere in the Vogosca area the Serbian forces had arrested one of his men. He told me to find him within that same day and to return the man to him, in Sarajevo, or else he would kill 40 Serbs who were in his custody at the hotel. Or maybe -- I don't remember whether the hotel was called Bosna or Evropa. I apologise. I forget the name of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the hotel. Describe briefly, please, the incident.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: All right. So I made numerous phone calls, calling people in Ilijas, Vogosca, Ilidza. He gave me the name of this man of his who was missing. I couldn't find the man. Earlier as he told me this, he put one of those Serbs on the phone and said, Let's have this Serb tell you about this. Vojo Milijas [phoen] took the phone. He was the director of the Privredna bank in Sarajevo, and while crying he said, Slobo, do something and save us. I did everything I could. The man we were looking for was simply missing. In the afternoon the commander called me again asking whether there was anything new. I said, No. And he said, Well, I'm taking over now. And I told him, Well, it's up to you now. Show us whether you're human or inhumane. This is where the conversation ended. Later on, I heard that Vojo Milijas had fled to Belgrade. I don't know about other people. I never spoke to Vojo Milijas again to inquire about the details, so I don't know what happened. It is possible that nobody died in that incident. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you have heard if 48 Serbs had been killed that day by this man?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Forgive me, but he didn't need to kill all 40 of them at once. He could have killed one by one, one a day. I never heard about an incident in which 40 Serbs were killed at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. And as far as you know, Mr. Vojo Milijas was clearly released because he went to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes, he fled to Belgrade after the war and then -- at any rate, the man is alive. He had been released.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I now want to move then off the question -- I'm sorry. You said it was these two incidents that made you speak to Mr. Stanisic. Did you speak to Mr. Stanisic about this question of dealing with exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Yes. When Minister Stanisic came, I told him, Minister, please let us establish a committee for exchange at the government level. I do not want to do this any longer. I had experienced two huge traumas and I wanted somebody else to take over to do that job. Several days later, certain Rajko Tolovic [phoen] arrived. I don't know whether he was appointed by the cabinet or by whom. He introduced him as deputy military prosecutor in Vlasenica. I handed over to him all of the documents concerning the exchange, and I was done with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was it that you spoke to Stanisic about replacing you, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, let's say mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And between dealing with the Vrace prisoners and mid-May, how many exchanges of prisoners all together do you think you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did four exchanges with Sime Grubisic plus the exchange, or whatever you want to call it, the freeing of 200 of Bosniaks and sending them off to Visoko. So as far as I remember I did the four exchanges plus this other event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want to move to some other aspects of your work, please. First of all, I want you to have a look, if you would, at -- sorry, I'll just get my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, 37, 22 -- oh. It has been corrected right now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you have a look, please, at a document with the 65 ter number 87.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's it, at least not in B/C/S. It's definitely not it. It should be -- the B/C/S version should be 2089524. See, it's a different date. No -- sorry, in that case -- it's the 17th of April I want, not the 3rd of April, both in English and B/C/S. That now says the 3rd of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Looking at the B/C/S please, Mr. Skipina, Can you tell us, somebody is signing on behalf of Mico Stanisic. Can you tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I see the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask, this is -- it's an order or a dispatch, I should -- to the CSBs. It's to do with people stealing property. How is it that you signed on behalf of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Minister Stanisic called me two or three times on the phone, saying that they would bring a dispatch to me. I think that it was in April. And then he would say, Please sign it so that it can be sent to the centres. I did sign it. These are the matters within the scope of the public security. The minister told me, I read it, and in relation to one dispatch, the minister told me, If have you any suggestions incorporate them into the dispatch and sign. And this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- well, this is the first thing. This is all connected with the public security, isn't it, not the state security, of which you were head?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So why was he asking you as head of state security to sign a document that related to public security matters? Why not Mr. Kljajic, for example?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that Kljajic was absent at that moment and that he couldn't sign the dispatch, and that the minister was also absent and couldn't sign the dispatch. And then, as the second under-secretary, the second person in charge within the MUP, he told me to sign the dispatch, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has not yet so far been exhibited, so can I ask it be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1252, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want to move next to a whole series of daily events, bulletins or the like. Now, Your Honours, I do not want to have go through everything single one of them. Some are signed, I think, by him and others by other people. Can I ask that if there's no objection, they simply -- I can give you the numbers after we've been through one or two and just have them all admitted and marked and explain what they are, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there likely to be an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't know what we are talking about. It is likely we don't have the objection, but I would like to know what -- what specific documents are we -- Ms. Korner has in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll put up one of them. Can we have up, please, document number 937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, I suppose, Ms. Korner, that what you are attempting to do is the practice we have sort of adopted of marking the batch according to one or two specimens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and you will see that they're all the same type of document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a documented dated 23red of April headed Daily Events Bulletin. It's got the stamp and it's, I think, says, Minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic. But can you tell us who signed that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: It's not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: And I don't know whose it is. I can't identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But before we move to the next one, can you tell us what these daily events bulletins were, daily reports they're sometimes called.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: There were daily events, bulletins, and daily reports which were intended for the people in leading positions to inform them about the events. And then when it came to more serious bulletins, then prime minister was also informed of them. However, in the list of addressees, if there were any external addressees, say cabinet members, then the bulletin would say that it was sent to the cabinet as well. If nothing of the sort was stated then it was meant for only internal use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But these daily events, reports, or bulletins were intended for people in leading positions, and by that, do you mean the -- the politicians or leading positions in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: There were no politicians in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry. You said, "these daily reports were intended for people in leading positions." Leading positions in the MUP or outside the municipal, for example, in the government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Those that do not contain any indication to whom they were copied were intended for senior staff in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And what was the purpose behind senior staff in the MUP getting these reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, that was their purpose, to provide as much information about developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And if Mico Stanisic didn't sign for some reason, and I think we'll come to ones that you did sign, would he be aware of the contents of these reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: If he signed under the report, it's only reasonable to assume that he was familiar with a particular bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it has his stamp and his typed signature but actually somebody like you had signed on his behalf, would he still be aware, would you sign without his permission to sign, or his instructions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: If a report was intended as internal information, then it was not particularly valuable as a document, and I could sign it or any other senior staff member could sign it because it did not have any particular importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, just for a moment, let's just have a look at this particular one even though you didn't sign it. Did you get these reports in your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I did not. But I'm familiar with those that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. If it was meant -- if these reports were meant for leaders -- those in leading positions in the MUP, did you hold a leading position in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I was nominally one of the leading people in the MUP, but in practice, the National Security Service was a separate service within the security system, and it was only nominally linked to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just -- the contents of this daily events bulletin, the young Predrag Mocevic was monstrously killed, or, rather, massacred by the Green Berets today in Sarajevo ... the autopsy report shows exactly how the butchers went around their -- abut their job, et cetera, et cetera. Is that sort of language that you expect in this period to be found in a police report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I would not expect it. But it was up to the person who did the writing. We did not have professional analysts in charge of writing these reports. I wouldn't say this is appropriate language, but it is also not appropriate for the media to name me and my son as the key throat-slitters in Pale. And my son who had been the subject of many death threats, has lived in Belgrade since 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it matters when his son left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina, I'm sorry, would you say this language was intended to incite hatred of non-Serbs amongst the police officers who were going to read it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Perhaps you could read that into it. But aren't the things that I'm mentioning about to you also inappropriate? I worked for a long time in Sarajevo, and I had friends among both Croats and Bosniaks, and they called me a throat-cutter; whereas, I saved many of these people. And that's -- you can't say that's propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of Mr. Stanisic saying, I'm not going to let a report in this sort of language go out under my name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Stanisic only very seldom. I don't know how he would react if a particular report came to his desk. So I cannot answer in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this particular report not signed by him by somebody else, but I'm go to go on to ones that are actually signed by him. I don't know whether I can have this exhibited on the way, as it were. I mean, he is familiar with these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we better see the other specimens that you intend to show first and then we'll come back to the question of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can I -- can I have it marked for identification, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1253 marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just for the sake of accuracy of the transcript 43, 13, I believe the witness said, I mentioned -- I'm mentioning about me. What the things that are mentioning about me are also inappropriate, and it is recorded as you. So it doesn't make sense like it is recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at document 942, please. Can we just ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. 30th of April. Could we have a look just at the bottom, the signature, again, somebody signing on behalf of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whose signature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: With 95 per cent certainty, I think it is Radomir Ninkovic. At the time, he was assistant minister for analysis and information in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have the second paragraph of that report down which says:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "According to reports received from the public security station of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, the town is now free and the situation is gradually becoming normal." What do you understand is meant by "the town is now free"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, in my understanding, it had been earlier attacked by Bosniak and Croat forces before Serbian authorities finally re-asserted their control over that area. That's how I would understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The town is now free. When it is being attacked, you say, by Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, I suppose because it says according to reports from the public security station of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, this town is now free, which means that it had been attacked by some forces. The members of the Croatian paramilitary forces had been disarmed, et cetera, et cetera, which means that some activity had taken place before and they now report the town is free again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it doesn't read to you that the very opposite, that the Bosniaks and Croats were in the town and the Serbs were attacking it, and that's how they freed it; that doesn't read that to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe you could read it that way too. I don't know what the situation was. Maybe you could read it that way. But I read it the way I already described.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When weren't you collecting intelligence from all these areas, as head of the SNB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I did not have any contact whatsoever with the national security sectors in Banja Luka and Doboj throughout my tenure, that is, up to the 3rd of July when I resigned. I had no communication whatsoever with the national security sector in Doboj and its leader Dusan Zivkovic all with Nedeljko Kesic in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll come on to your contacts with Mr. Kesic, but, I'm sorry, you're saying that Samac -- Samac came under Doboj, because it certainly didn't come under Banja Luka, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: That's right. It was under Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say you had no contacts with them, you were receiving -- reports were being received, weren't they, from these areas both from Doboj and Banja Luka because if we go through these daily reports we'll see there was information. So what do you mean, you had no contact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SKIPINA
utterances.text: I said sometime ago that the National Security Service was a separate service which has its own rules. It was dealing with intelligence and counter-intelligence work, anti-terrorist activity against attacks from abroad, and this service does not communicate in open text, not even on the telephone.
